card.text: 3 lines. 3 types. Guess all three.
card.code:
typeof null
typeof NaN
typeof []

caption:
Comment your guess first. Answer below.

.
.
.

"object", "number", "object".

typeof null is "object" because of a bug in the very first version of JavaScript. Fixing it would break old websites, so it stays.

NaN is a special value of the number type. Its name says "not a number", its type says number.

Arrays are objects. To check for an array, use Array.isArray([]) which returns true.

Source: MDN, typeof operator.

How many did you get?

card.text:
useMemo is not free.

On every render React still compares the dependency array and keeps the old value in memory.

Wrap the one slow calculation. Not every variable.

caption:
I review a lot of React code where every value is wrapped in useMemo "for performance".

For cheap work like filtering 20 items or joining two strings, the comparison costs about as much as just doing the work again.

How to decide: measure first. React's docs suggest wrapping a calculation in console.time and memoizing only if it takes a noticeable amount of time (around 1 ms or more).

Source: react.dev, useMemo.

Where have you seen useMemo overused?

card.text:
HTTP forgets you after every request.

Cookies are how a website remembers you are logged in:
card.code:
# server, after login
Set-Cookie: sid=a1b2; HttpOnly

# browser, every next request
Cookie: sid=a1b2

caption:
HTTP is stateless: each request arrives with no memory of the last one.

After you log in, the server sends a Set-Cookie header. The browser stores it and automatically attaches it to every later request to that site. The server looks up sid=a1b2 and knows it's you.

HttpOnly means JavaScript on the page cannot read the cookie, so a malicious script can't steal it.

Source: MDN, Using HTTP cookies.

Open DevTools → Application → Cookies on any site you're logged into and find yours.

card.text:
First offer. Pick one:

A) ₹6 LPA at a 40-person product startup
B) ₹9 LPA at a large IT services company

Which one, and why?

caption:
There's no single right answer. It depends on what you want from your first two years: learning speed, stability, brand name, or money for your family right now.

I'm interested in the reasoning more than the letter.

If you've already made this choice, tell us how it turned out.

card.text:
== converts types before comparing. === doesn't.

That's why these surprise people:
card.code:
0 == ''            // true
'1' == 1           // true
null == undefined  // true
0 === ''           // false
'1' === 1          // false

caption:
With ==, JavaScript first converts both sides to a common type, then compares. '' becomes 0, '1' becomes 1, and the results look random until you know the rules.

=== compares type and value with no conversion, so what you see is what you get.

Rule most teams follow: always use ===. The one common exception is value == null, which matches both null and undefined in one check.

Source: MDN, Equality comparisons and sameness.

card.text:
AI probably won't take your job this year.

But a teammate who ships the same feature in 2 days instead of 5, because they use it well, will get the interesting projects.

caption:
The real competition isn't you vs the AI. It's you vs other developers who learned to use it properly.

Using it properly means: giving it the right context, reviewing every change, writing the tests, and knowing when its answer is wrong.

That's a skill. It takes practice like any other.

What's one task where AI genuinely saves you time today?

card.text:
|| replaces every falsy value.
?? replaces only null and undefined.

That difference breaks real apps:

caption:
Imagine a cart where the user set quantity to 0. With ||, your default kicks in and they suddenly have 10 items.

|| treats 0, '', false and NaN as "missing". Sometimes those are real values.

?? (nullish coalescing) only falls back when the value is null or undefined.

Pair it with optional chaining: user?.address?.city ?? 'Unknown'.

Source: MDN, Nullish coalescing operator.

Search your project for "|| 0" and "|| ''". Some of them should be ??.

card.text:
What's the worst bug you shipped to production?

What broke, how long it took to notice, and what you changed after.

caption:
Every experienced developer has at least one of these stories. Freshers rarely hear them, so they think seniors never break things.

Share yours. Juniors learn more from these than from any tutorial.

I'll pick a few and write a breakdown of what each one teaches.

card.text:
Temperature controls how random an AI model's answers are.

Low (0 to 0.3): same question, nearly the same answer. Use for code, JSON, extraction.

High (0.8+): more varied wording. Use for brainstorming names or ideas.

caption:
The model picks each next word from a list of likely options. Temperature changes how often it picks the less likely ones.

Example: ask for a product description 3 times at high temperature and you get 3 different versions. Ask a model to return JSON at high temperature and you get more broken JSON.

Not every model or app lets you change it, and some newer models fix it for you. When an API does expose it, start low for anything a program will read.

Source: provider API docs (OpenAI, Anthropic), temperature parameter.

card.text:
Flexbox lays things out in one direction.
Grid lays things out in two.

Navbar items in a row → flex.
A gallery of product cards in rows and columns → grid.

caption:
A quick test: do you care about lining things up across rows AND columns at the same time? Use grid. Only along one line? Use flex.

You can mix them. A grid for the page layout, flex inside each card for its title and button.

Grid one-liner worth saving:
grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr));
That gives a responsive card gallery with no media queries.

Source: MDN, Relationship of grid layout to other layout methods.

card.text: Two counters from the same function. What prints?

caption:
Comment your guess first. Answer below.

.
.
.

3 1

Each call to counter() creates a new n. The returned arrow function keeps access to its own n even after counter() has finished. That's a closure.

a has been called 3 times in total, so its n is 3. b has its own n and was called once, so 1.

This is exactly how private state worked before classes, and how React hooks remember values between renders.

Source: MDN, Closures.

card.text:
Which way do you learn more?

A) You write the code, AI reviews it.
B) AI writes the code, you review it.

caption:
Both are fast. They train very different muscles.

A makes you struggle first and then shows you what you missed.
B makes you a reviewer early, which is what senior work looks like, but you can skip the struggle that builds intuition.

I have a clear opinion for students vs working devs. Tell me yours first.

card.text:
SQL or NoSQL? Look at your data, not the hype.

Orders, payments, users linked to each other → SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL). Joins and transactions keep them consistent.

Each record has a different shape (product specs, event logs) → a document database like MongoDB.

caption:
A transaction means: several changes happen together or not at all. Debit one account and credit another, never only one of them. Relational databases are built around this.

Document databases store each record as JSON-like documents, so a phone and a T-shirt can have completely different fields without schema changes.

Many real products use both. Payments in Postgres, activity logs somewhere else.

If you're learning backend, start with SQL. It shows up in almost every interview.

Source: PostgreSQL and MongoDB documentation.

card.text:
2 DSA problems a day for 90 days = 180 problems.

20 problems the night before the placement test = panic.

Consistency beats intensity.

caption:
180 problems spread over 3 months is enough to see most common patterns: two pointers, sliding window, hashing, BFS/DFS, binary search, basic DP.

The spacing matters. Your brain needs sleep between practice sessions to actually keep what you learned.

Small plan: 1 easy + 1 medium every day, same time, and revisit any problem you couldn't solve after 3 days.

When does your placement season start?

card.text:
Inside a regular function callback, this is NOT your object.

An arrow function uses this from where it was written:

caption:
Both callbacks live inside the start() method of a timer object.

A regular function gets its own this, decided by how it is called. setInterval calls it with this set to the global object (window in browsers). Never your timer.

Arrow functions don't have their own this. They use the this of the surrounding code, which is the timer.

The old fix was const self = this. Arrow functions made it unnecessary.

Source: MDN, Arrow function expressions.

card.text:
A common React slowdown I see in code reviews:

one Context holds user, theme AND the search box text.

Type one letter → every component using that Context re-renders.

caption:
Every component that reads a Context re-renders when that Context's value changes. If fast-changing state (like input text) lives next to slow-changing state (user, theme), everything pays for every keystroke.

Fixes:
Keep input state local to the component that owns it.
Split contexts: one for user, one for theme.
Memoize the context value object.

React DevTools → Profiler → "Highlight updates" shows you exactly what re-renders.

Source: react.dev, useContext (optimizing re-renders).

card.text:
An embedding turns text into a list of numbers.

Texts with similar meaning get similar numbers.

So a search for "cheap phone" can find a product called "budget mobile", with zero matching words.

caption:
Normal search matches words. Embedding search (semantic search) matches meaning.

How it works:
1. Turn every product description into an embedding once and store it.
2. Turn the user's query into an embedding.
3. Find the stored embeddings closest to the query.

This is step 1 of RAG: it finds the right paragraphs before the AI model writes an answer.

You can try it with a free embedding model and a few hundred rows. A great weekend project for your resume.

Source: OpenAI and Hugging Face embedding guides.

card.text:
Students: what's harder for you, DSA or building real projects?

Working devs: which one helped you more AFTER you got the job?

caption:
I hear this debate every week from students I mentor.

I'd love to see the two groups answer side by side. Mention whether you're a student or working, and for how long.

card.text: I copied the object. Why did the original change?

caption:
Comment your guess first. Answer below.

.
.
.

30.

Spread makes a shallow copy. b is a new object, but b.user and a.user point to the same inner object. Change one, both see it.

For a deep copy, use structuredClone(a). It copies nested objects, arrays, Dates and Maps. It cannot copy functions or DOM elements.

In React this matters a lot: mutating nested state this way is why the screen sometimes doesn't update.

Source: MDN, structuredClone() and Shallow copy.

card.text:
Never store passwords.

Store a slow, salted hash (bcrypt or Argon2).

If your database leaks, attackers should get gibberish, not your users' passwords.

caption:
A hash is one-way: you can check a password against it, but you can't turn it back into the password.

Why slow? Fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 can be guessed billions of times per second on a GPU. bcrypt and Argon2 are designed to be slow and expensive to guess.

Why salted? A random value added per user means two people with the password "123456" get different hashes.

Never encrypt passwords (encryption can be reversed) and never write your own.

Source: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet.

card.text: Sorting 4 numbers. What could go wrong?

caption:
Comment your guess first. Answer below.

.
.
.

[1, 10, 100, 9]

Without a compare function, sort() converts every item to a string and sorts alphabetically. "10" comes before "9" because "1" comes before "9".

Fix: [10, 9, 1, 100].sort((a, b) => a - b) gives [1, 9, 10, 100].

Also: sort() changes the original array. If you need a sorted copy, use toSorted() in modern browsers.

Source: MDN, Array.prototype.sort().

card.text:
Ask AI to EXPLAIN the error before you ask it to FIX the error.

"Fix this" solves the bug once.
"Explain this" means you'll recognise it next time without help.

caption:
Same tool, two different outcomes.

Try this prompt next time: "Explain what this error means, why my code causes it, and how I could have found it myself. Don't fix it yet."

Then fix it yourself. Ask for the fix only if you're still stuck.

It takes 2 extra minutes. After a month you'll notice you need AI for errors much less often.

card.text: count starts at 0. The user clicks once. What's count after the render?

caption:
Comment your guess first. Answer below.

.
.
.

1, not 3.

Inside this click, count is 0 the whole time. All three calls say "set it to 0 + 1". React batches them, and the result is 1.

When the next value depends on the previous one, pass a function:
setCount(c => c + 1)
React queues these and runs each with the latest value, so three calls give 3.

Source: react.dev, Queueing a series of state updates.

card.text:
A fresher asks you which framework to learn first in 2026.

React, Angular or Vue?

One line, with your reason.

caption:
Job listings, college projects and company stacks in India all pull in different directions.

I want answers from people who hire or work on these daily. Mention which one you use at work.

card.text:
Hit an API too often and it answers 429 Too Many Requests.

The response often tells you how long to wait:
card.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30

caption:
APIs limit requests per user or per key (for example, 100 per minute) so one client can't slow down everyone else. This is rate limiting.

What your frontend should do:
Read Retry-After (seconds) and wait that long.
If it's missing, retry with exponential backoff: wait 1s, then 2s, then 4s.
Never retry in a tight loop. That makes the problem worse.

Also a common cause: a useEffect with a missing dependency array firing the same request on every render.

Source: MDN, 429 Too Many Requests.

card.text:
Your resume is not a list of technologies.

"React, Redux, Tailwind" says nothing.

"Cut page load from 6s to 2s by lazy-loading images" says everything.

caption:
Every fresher's resume has the same skills section. Recruiters skim past it.

What stands out is a result: what you changed, how you did it, and a number that shows it worked.

Format for each project bullet:
Did X, using Y, which improved Z (with a number).

No real numbers yet? Measure your own project with Lighthouse before and after a change. Now you have one.

Rewrite one bullet today and post it in the comments. I'll give feedback on a few.

card.text: If it happens because the user clicked, it belongs in the click handler. Not in useEffect.

caption:
The useEffect version is harder to follow and can fire twice or at the wrong time (for example, when the component mounts with sent already true).

React's own docs: if code runs because of a specific interaction, put it in that event handler. Use effects only to sync with things outside React, like a timer, a WebSocket or a browser API.

Quick test: can you name the user action that causes it? Then it's an event handler.

Source: react.dev, You Might Not Need an Effect.

card.text:
Has AI made you a better developer, or just a faster one?

They're not the same thing.

caption:
Faster: you ship the same work in less time.
Better: you understand more, make fewer mistakes, and can solve problems you couldn't before.

It's possible to get one without the other.

Be honest in the comments. Which one is it for you?

card.text: Asked an AI model for JSON? Don't trust the shape. Validate it:

caption:
Models usually return what you ask for. Usually isn't good enough for code that runs in production.

A missing field or a number where you expected a string will crash your UI somewhere far away from the actual cause.

This uses Zod, a validation library. Out.parse throws a clear error the moment the shape is wrong, so you can retry the request or show a fallback.

Many AI APIs now also support structured outputs (you pass a JSON schema). Still validate. It's one line.

Source: zod.dev.

card.text:
Your React app cannot keep a secret.

Every VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable is copied into the JavaScript bundle. Anyone can read it in DevTools.

API keys belong on a server.

caption:
Build tools replace those env variables with their actual values at build time. They end up as plain text inside the .js files your users download.

Open DevTools → Sources on your deployed app and search for your key. If it's there, it's public.

Fix: call the third-party API from your own backend (or a serverless function), keep the key in the server's environment, and let the frontend call your backend.

Source: Vite docs (Env Variables) and Next.js docs (Environment Variables).

card.text:
position: sticky not sticking? Check two things:

1. Did you set top?
2. Does any parent have overflow: hidden or auto?

caption:
Sticky needs a threshold. Without top (or bottom, left, right) it behaves like position: relative.

Sticky also sticks inside its nearest scrolling ancestor. If a parent has overflow: hidden, auto or scroll, the element sticks inside that parent instead of the page. Often it looks like it isn't working at all.

Debug fast: in DevTools, walk up the parents in the Elements panel and look for overflow in the Computed tab.

Source: MDN, position (sticky positioning).

card.text:
Learn one SQL database properly before you learn five NoSQL ones.

JOINs, indexes and transactions come up in almost every backend interview.

caption:
Frontend devs moving to backend often jump straight to whatever is trending.

SQL has been around for decades and it isn't going anywhere. Postgres alone will teach you data modelling, query performance (EXPLAIN), and how to keep data consistent.

A good first project: a small expense tracker with users, categories and expenses. Three tables, real JOINs, real indexes.

Which database did you learn first?

card.text: var and let, both used before they're declared. What happens?

caption:
Comment your guess first. Answer below.

.
.
.

First log: undefined.
Second log: ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization.

Both declarations are hoisted (registered at the start of the scope). But var is also set to undefined right away, while let and const stay uninitialised until their line runs. The gap is called the temporal dead zone.

The error is the better behaviour. Silent undefined values hide bugs.

Source: MDN, Hoisting and let.

card.text:
A fresher taking 2 hours on a bug: normal.

Taking 2 days without asking anyone: the actual problem.

Try for 1-2 hours. Write down what you tried. Then ask.

caption:
Juniors stay quiet because they don't want to look slow. Seniors would much rather spend 10 minutes unblocking you than find out on day 3.

Writing down what you tried does two things. Often you spot the answer while writing it. If not, your senior can skip the obvious questions and help you faster.

Template: "I'm trying to X. I expected Y, I got Z. I've tried A and B."

Save this for your first job.

card.text:
User double-clicks "Pay ₹499". Two requests reach the server.

Did you charge them twice?

Idempotency keys prevent it: the client sends the same unique key with both requests, and the server processes that key only once.

caption:
Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.

GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by design. POST is not, which is why "create payment" needs extra care.

Payment APIs like Stripe support an Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the key with the result and returns the same result for a repeat.

Frontend side: disable the button after the first click too. But never rely only on the frontend, because retries also happen on flaky networks.

Source: MDN (Idempotent) and Stripe API docs (Idempotent requests).

card.text:
An AI answer that sounds confident is not an AI answer that is correct.

One follow-up catches a lot of mistakes:

"What would make this answer wrong?"

caption:
Models write in the same confident tone whether they're right or guessing.

Asking for the weak points makes the model look at its own answer again. Often it mentions an edge case, an outdated API, or an assumption about your setup.

Other good follow-ups:
"Which part of this are you least sure about?"
"Show me where in the docs this is described."

Then verify the important parts yourself.

card.text:
Google measures your page's user experience with 3 numbers. "Good" means:

LCP ≤ 2.5 s: main content visible
INP ≤ 200 ms: page responds to taps
CLS ≤ 0.1: layout doesn't jump around

caption:
These are the Core Web Vitals.

LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): when the biggest image or text block appears.
INP (Interaction to Next Paint): the delay between a tap and the screen updating.
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): how much things move while loading.

The thresholds are measured at the 75th percentile of real visits, so your slowest users count.

Check any site at pagespeed.web.dev. Try your college website.

Source: web.dev, Web Vitals.

card.text:
A page is slow. What do you open first?

A) Network tab
B) Performance tab
C) Lighthouse

And why that one?

caption:
Each one answers a different question. Picking the right first tool saves a lot of time.

I'll share how I approach it in a follow-up, step by step, with a real slow page.

Your answer first.

card.text:
map returns a new array.
forEach returns undefined.

caption:
Use map when you want a new array built from the old one (rendering a list in React, converting prices).

Use forEach when you only want side effects and don't need a result (logging, pushing to analytics).

Common bug: using map, ignoring its result, and getting an ESLint warning. Or using forEach inside JSX and rendering nothing.

Neither one works with await the way you expect. For async loops, use for...of or Promise.all.

Source: MDN, Array.prototype.map() and forEach().

card.text:
My favourite AI prompt for learning anything:

"Explain this like I'm a 2nd-year B.Tech student. Then ask me one question to check if I understood."

caption:
The first half gets you a simple explanation. The second half is the important part.

When you have to answer a question, you find out right away whether you actually understood it or just nodded along.

If you get it wrong, ask it to explain the part you missed in a different way.

Try it today on a topic you've been avoiding. Event loop? Indexes? Closures?

card.text:
Why do AI coding agents keep asking "Allow this command?"

Because an agent that can run
rm -rf build/
can also run
rm -rf ~/

The permission prompt is your last review step. Read it.

caption:
An agent's tools (run shell commands, edit files, call APIs) are real actions on your machine or your accounts.

Good habits:
Allow read-only commands freely. Read anything that deletes, pushes, or sends data.
Run agents inside the project folder, not your home directory.
Use git, so every file change can be undone.
Never paste secrets into the chat.

This idea is called least privilege: give a tool only the access its task needs.

Source: OWASP, principle of least privilege.

card.text:
Unplug your mouse and try to fill your own signup form.

Can you reach every field with Tab? Submit with Enter? See where focus is?

If not, some of your users can't sign up.

caption:
Keyboard users include people with motor disabilities, screen reader users and plenty of power users.

The usual problems:
Clickable divs that Tab skips.
outline: none with no replacement, so focus is invisible.
Custom dropdowns that ignore arrow keys.

Most are fixed by using real elements: <button>, <input>, <select>, <form>.

Five-minute test, no tools needed. Try it on your project tonight.

Source: WCAG 2.2, Keyboard (2.1.1) and Focus Visible (2.4.7).

card.text:
Inside a <form>, a <button> is type="submit" by default.

So your Cancel button submits the form.
card.code:
<form onSubmit={save}>
  <button>Save</button>
  <button type="button">
    Cancel
  </button>
</form>

caption:
Without type="button", clicking Cancel triggers the form's submit. Your save handler runs and, without e.preventDefault(), the page reloads.

Rule: inside a form, every button that should not submit needs type="button".

Bonus: because Save is a real submit button, pressing Enter in any input also submits the form. You get that for free.

Source: MDN, <button> (type attribute).

card.text:
You're a frontend dev learning backend.

Node.js, Java (Spring), Go or Python?

Pick one and give one reason.

caption:
Node lets you reuse JavaScript. Java dominates big Indian enterprises. Go is popular in infra and startups. Python is everywhere in AI.

All four get people hired.

Tell me which one you picked and whether you'd choose it again.

card.text:
Never commit your .env file.

Bots scan public GitHub repos for leaked keys. Once pushed, assume it is stolen.
card.code:
# .gitignore
.env
.env.local

# commit this instead
.env.example

caption:
A .env file holds secrets: database URLs, API keys, payment keys. Deleting it in the next commit doesn't help: it's still in git history.

Safe setup:
Add .env to .gitignore before your first commit.
Commit .env.example with the variable names and fake values.
In production, set real values in your hosting platform's settings.

Already leaked one? Revoke and regenerate the key first. Cleaning history comes second.

Source: GitHub docs, About secret scanning.

card.text:
Read your teammates' pull requests at your first job. Even the ones you're not reviewing.

It's free mentorship from every senior on the team.

caption:
Every PR shows how someone experienced broke down a problem, named things, handled errors and wrote tests. The review comments show what the team actually cares about.

20 minutes a day of reading merged PRs teaches you the codebase faster than any onboarding doc.

When something confuses you, ask in the PR thread. Most seniors are happy to explain.

card.text: A rejected promise, a catch, and two thens. What prints?
card.code:
Promise.reject('x')
  .then(() => console.log(1))
  .catch(() => console.log(2))
  .then(() => console.log(3));

caption:
Comment your guess first. Answer below.

.
.
.

2, then 3.

The first then is skipped because the promise is rejected. catch handles the error and returns normally, so the chain is back on the success path. The last then runs.

This is why one catch at the end of a chain is common: it handles an error from any step above it. A then after a catch always runs unless the catch throws again.

Source: MDN, Using promises (Error handling).

card.text:
An AI coding tool is only as safe as your tests.

No tests = no quick way to know if its "small refactor" broke checkout.

caption:
Tests turn "looks right to me" into a pass or fail you can check in seconds.

They also help the AI itself: agents can run the tests, read the failures, and fix their own mistakes before you even look.

Start small: one test per important user flow (login, add to cart, checkout). That alone catches the worst breakages.

Does your current project have tests?

card.text:
Why send a 1600px image to a 400px phone screen?

With srcset, the browser picks the right size:

caption:
srcset lists the same image at different widths (400w means 400 pixels wide). sizes tells the browser how wide the image will be shown on screen.

The browser then downloads only the one it needs, taking screen size and pixel density into account. A budget phone on mobile data gets the small file.

src stays as the fallback for very old browsers.

Frameworks like Next.js generate this for you with their Image component. Now you know what it's doing.

Source: MDN, Responsive images.

card.text:
Accessibility is not a feature for "a few users".

Captions help on a noisy train.
High contrast helps on a phone in sunlight.
Keyboard support helps when your trackpad dies.

caption:
Accessibility work is usually framed as helping people with permanent disabilities. It does, and that alone is reason enough.

But the same fixes help everyone in temporary situations: an injured arm, a bright screen, a slow connection, a loud room.

And in many countries it's a legal requirement for public-facing sites.

Which one does your current project fail at?

Source: W3C WAI, Introduction to Web Accessibility.

card.text:
Want an AI model to work with your company's data? Try these in order:

1. Better prompt + examples
2. RAG: fetch the right documents into the prompt
3. Fine-tuning: retrain the model

Most teams never need step 3.

caption:
Prompting is free and instant. Try it until it clearly isn't enough.

RAG solves "the model doesn't know our data". The data stays in your database, so it's always up to date and you can show sources.

Fine-tuning changes the model itself. It helps with style, format or a very specific task. It costs money, needs good training data, and doesn't keep up with data that changes daily.

Interview tip: if asked "how would you build a support bot for our docs", start with RAG and say why.

Source: OpenAI and Anthropic docs on prompt engineering and fine-tuning.

card.text:
You can send one message to yourself in 1st year of college.

What's the one thing about coding you'd tell yourself?

caption:
Students reading this are in that exact position right now.

Give them your best advice: what to start earlier, what to ignore, what to stop worrying about.

I'll compile the best answers into one post.

card.text:
Ten console.logs to find one bug?

Put debugger; on the line. With DevTools open, the code pauses there and you can inspect every variable.

caption:
While paused, you can hover any variable to see its value, step to the next line, step into a function, and see the full call stack (who called this function and from where).

Even better than editing code: click a line number in DevTools → Sources to set a breakpoint. Right-click it to make it conditional, like "only pause when i.price is undefined".

console.log is fine. Breakpoints are faster when you don't know where the bug is.

Source: Chrome DevTools docs, Pause your code with breakpoints.

card.text:
Your API returns res.json(user).

Congratulations. You just sent the password hash, the email and the internal fields to the browser.

Pick the fields you return.

caption:
The frontend may only show the user's name, but the Network tab shows the entire response to anyone.

Return exactly what the screen needs:
res.json({ id: user.id, name: user.name })

Most ORMs and frameworks have a way to select or exclude fields. Use it as a default, not an afterthought.

OWASP listed this as "Excessive Data Exposure" in its 2019 API Top 10. The 2023 list folds it into "Broken Object Property Level Authorization".

Source: OWASP API Security Top 10.

card.text:
Getting live updates into the browser:

Polling: ask the server every few seconds.
SSE: server pushes updates over one HTTP connection.
WebSocket: both sides send anytime.

Notifications → SSE. Chat or games → WebSocket.

caption:
Polling is simplest and fine for things that change every few minutes. But most requests return "nothing new".

Server-Sent Events (SSE): one long-lived connection, the server streams events down. It reconnects automatically. Streaming AI responses token by token often uses this.

WebSockets: a two-way connection. Needed when the client also sends a lot in real time.

Start with the simplest option that meets the need.

Source: MDN, Server-sent events and The WebSocket API.

card.text:
Should a fresher write "Prompt Engineering" on their resume?

Yes, no, or only with a project to prove it?

caption:
Recruiters and interviewers especially, I want your view.

Is it a real skill worth listing, a buzzword that hurts more than it helps, or somewhere in between?

card.text: Two different objects as keys. What prints?

caption:
Comment your guess first. Answer below.

.
.
.

'second'.

Object keys are strings (or symbols). Both b and c get converted to the string "[object Object]", so they're the same key. The second assignment overwrites the first.

If you need objects as keys, use a Map:
const m = new Map();
m.set(b, 'first');
Map keeps the actual object as the key.

Source: MDN, Map (Objects vs. Maps).

card.text:
Learn DevTools before you learn another framework.

Elements: why the layout broke.
Network: what the API actually returned.
Console: what threw.

You'll use it every working day.

caption:
Frameworks change every few years. The browser's tools have been the core debugging kit for over a decade, and they keep getting better.

Three skills to practise this week:
Edit CSS live in Elements until it looks right, then copy it back.
In Network, inspect a failing request's status code, request body and response.
Use breakpoints in Sources instead of console.log.

Which panel do you use the least?

card.text: Heavy calculation freezing your UI? Move it to a Web Worker. It runs on a separate thread, so clicks and scrolling stay smooth.

caption:
JavaScript on the page runs on one main thread, which also handles clicks, typing and painting. A 2-second loop there means 2 seconds of frozen page.

A Worker runs your script in the background. You send it data with postMessage and get the result back in onmessage.

Workers can't touch the DOM. They're for pure computation: parsing a big file, filtering a large list, image processing.

Source: MDN, Using Web Workers.

card.text:
Stuck finding a project idea?

Find something broken in your college: the canteen queue, the notice board, the lost-and-found.

Build the fix. Now you have a project, a story for interviews, and real users.

caption:
Interviewers hear about the same todo apps and Netflix clones all day.

A project with real users gives you real problems: people using it wrong, slow phones, feature requests, bugs you didn't predict. Those are the stories that stand out in interviews.

It doesn't need to be big. Ten students using it every day is enough.

What would you fix in your college first?

card.title:
Delete the first todo.
Why does its text stay behind?
card.note: A key says which item is which. An [[index]] changes when the list does.

caption:
Use the array index as a key in a machine coding round and your todo list breaks the first time someone deletes an item.

Look at the card. Three todos, each with an input. Delete the first one.

React matches list items by key, not by content. Before the delete the keys were 0, 1, 2. After it they are 0, 1. So React decides the item with key 2 was removed and keeps the inputs for keys 0 and 1 as they were. The first input on screen still shows the text you just deleted.

With key={t.id}, the key stays with the todo, and React removes the right input.

An index is only safe when the list never reorders, filters or deletes.

Source: react.dev, Rendering Lists.

card.text:
In 2026, writing code is the easy part.

[[Reading code]] is the job.

caption:
AI can now write the first draft of most features.

What it can't do is tell you whether that draft is right for your codebase, your users and your edge cases.

That's reading: someone else's code, the AI's code, your own code from six months ago.

Start this week: pick one open source repo you use and read one file a day. Just read it.

card.text:
Your production site might be shipping its [[source code]].

Open DevTools → Sources on your live site.
See your src/ folder with readable code? That's source maps.

caption:
Source maps link your minified bundle back to the original files. Great for debugging, but if they're public, anyone can read your original code, comments included.

Some setups have shipped them to production by default. Create React App did.

Check your own site. If you see your src folder:
- turn them off for production, or
- upload them only to your error tracker (like Sentry) instead of serving them.

Then search the bundle for anything that looks like a key. Frontend code is never a place for secrets.

Source: MDN, Use a source map (Firefox DevTools) and your bundler's build.sourcemap docs.

card.title:
AI wrote this timer.
Why does it stop at 1?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: The callback saw [[sec = 0]] forever. The updater reads the latest value.

caption:
Your AI assistant wrote a seconds counter. It has cleanup, it compiles, and it shows 1 forever. Would you approve it?

Look at the card. The effect runs once because of the empty dependency array. The interval callback was created during that first render, when sec was 0. So every second it calls setSec(0 + 1), and React gets 1 again and again.

The fix is to pass a function: setSec((s) => s + 1). React gives it the latest value each time, so the callback never needs to read sec.

No error, no warning, and the code looks clean. That's why it slips through review.

Source: react.dev, useState (updating state based on the previous state).

card.title:
Open and close this modal 10 times.
How many resize listeners are left?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: An effect that subscribes to something must [[unsubscribe]] in its cleanup.

caption:
Interviewers like this one because the code works perfectly in a demo.

Look at the card. Every time the modal opens, the effect adds a resize listener to window. When the modal closes, nothing removes it. Ten opens later, ten listeners are still attached, each one holding on to an old copy of the component.

The fix is the function you return from the effect. React calls it when the component unmounts, so the listener goes away with the modal.

This is also why React's StrictMode runs effects twice in development: a missing cleanup shows up right away instead of months later.

Source: react.dev, Synchronizing with Effects (adding cleanup).

card.text:
Your first job won't define your career.

What you learn in your [[first 2 years]] will.

caption:
Freshers stress for months over which company to join.

A few years later, nobody asks where your first job was. They ask what you can build, debug and own.

A smaller company where you ship every week can teach more than a big brand where you wait months for your first real task.

Pick the place where you'll learn the most. The salary catches up.

card.text:
Two developers. Same AI tool.

One ships fast.
One ships fast [[and can explain every line in review]].

Guess who gets promoted.

caption:
AI raised the floor. Everyone can produce working code quickly now.

What separates people is what happens after: reviewing the output, catching the edge case, explaining a decision to a teammate, owning the bug when it shows up in production.

Speed gets noticed. Understanding gets trusted.

What's one thing you always check before you commit AI-written code?

card.title:
AI made the effect async.
Would you merge it?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: An effect must return nothing or a [[cleanup function]]. An async function returns a promise.

caption:
AI tools write this all the time because it reads naturally.

Look at the card. An async function always returns a promise. React expects an effect to return either nothing or a cleanup function, so it warns in development. Worse, you've lost the one place where cleanup could go.

The fix: keep the effect synchronous and define an async function inside it, then call it.

Then add what the AI usually skips. If url changes quickly, an older response can arrive last and overwrite the newer one. The React docs fix that with a flag: set let ignore = false in the effect, set it to true in the cleanup, and skip setData when it's true.

Source: react.dev, Synchronizing with Effects (fetching data).

card.title:
Why does this API get called
on every single render?

panels.label: Common answer

card.note: Dependencies are compared by reference. A new object is a [[new dependency]].

caption:
Write this in a machine coding round and the Network tab fills up while the interviewer watches.

Look at the card. filters is created again on every render. It has the same values, but it's a new object, and React compares dependencies with Object.is, which checks the reference.

New object, so the effect runs. If fetchList sets state, that causes a render, which creates a new object, which runs the effect again.

The fix: depend on the primitive values the effect actually uses. Build the object inside the effect.

If you need the object outside too, useMemo can keep the same reference between renders.

Source: react.dev, Removing Effect Dependencies.

card.text:
Service company to product company is not a jump.

It's [[6 months of boring consistency]].

caption:
No single course or trick makes the switch.

What works is dull: one or two DSA problems a day, one real project you can explain end to end, and mock interviews before the real ones.

Most people quit in week three, when progress feels invisible.

The ones who switch are usually the ones who kept going through the boring middle.

card.text:
First offer. Pick one:

A) ₹5 LPA, remote, 15-person startup
B) ₹7 LPA, in-office, large MNC in Pune

[[Which one, and why?]]

caption:
There's no single right answer. It depends on what matters most to you right now: learning speed, mentorship in person, stability, or money for your family.

Remote at your first job is a real trade-off. You get flexibility, but learning from seniors is harder when you can't sit next to them.

If you've made a choice like this, how did it turn out?

card.title:
Payment failed.
Why did the user see "Order placed"?
card.note: A [[catch]] handles the error and returns a fresh, successful promise.

caption:
The AI put catch first "to handle errors early". It reads fine. Would you merge it?

Look at the card. When pay rejects, catch runs and shows "Failed". But catch also returns a new promise, and because the handler didn't throw, that promise resolves successfully. So the next then runs too. The user sees "Failed" and then "Order placed".

Order matters in a promise chain. Put the success step first and catch last, so a failure skips the success step.

With async/await it's harder to get wrong: put the success toast inside the try block, right after await pay(cart).

Source: MDN, Promise.prototype.catch().

card.title:
Click Cancel.
Why did the form get submitted?
card.note: Inside a form, every button is [[type="submit"]] unless you say otherwise.

caption:
This bug shows up in almost every machine coding round that has a form.

Look at the card. The Cancel button has an onClick that closes the modal. But it's a button inside a form with no type, and the default type of a button in a form is submit.

So one click runs close and then submits the form. The task gets saved even though the user pressed Cancel.

The fix is one attribute: type="button" on every button that shouldn't submit. Writing type="submit" on the real submit button makes your intent obvious to the next reader.

Source: MDN, The Button element (type attribute).

card.text:
Tutorial: 12 minutes.
Same feature in your own project: 2 days.

That gap is [[where you actually learn]].

caption:
A tutorial hides every hard decision: folder structure, error states, the API that returns something unexpected, the bug that only happens on refresh.

Your own project makes you face all of them.

So when your "simple" feature takes two days, don't feel slow. That's the part the tutorial skipped, and it's the part interviews ask about.

card.text:
Open your live app.
Open the Console.
Log in.

See user objects, tokens or API responses printed there?

So can [[everyone else]].

caption:
console.log calls written during development often ship to production. Anyone who opens DevTools can read them: user emails, auth tokens, full API responses.

Two fixes:
- remove them before merging (ESLint's no-console rule catches them)
- strip them at build time with your bundler's minifier settings

And never log a token, even while debugging. Logs get copied, screenshotted and pasted into AI chats.

Try it on your project tonight. It takes two minutes.

Source: ESLint docs, no-console rule.

card.title:
Two users, two carts.
Why do they share one?

panels.label: What I'd merge

card.note: Plain object keys become strings. Every object becomes [["[object Object]"]].

caption:
An AI assistant used a plain object as a lookup table, keyed by user objects. The tests used one user, so they passed.

Look at the card. Plain object keys are always strings (or symbols). userA and userB are objects, so JavaScript turns both into the same string: "[object Object]". The second assignment overwrites the first. Both users now share one cart.

A Map accepts any value as a key, including objects, and compares them by identity. userA and userB stay separate.

The other fix is to key the object by something that's already a string, like user.id.

Source: MDN, Map (objects vs maps).

card.title:
"All saved!" shows up
before anything is saved. Why?

panels.label: What gets you selected

card.note: [[forEach]] ignores the promises your callback returns.

caption:
Use await inside forEach in an interview and the follow-up question is always "so when does the toast show?"

Look at the card. The await works inside each callback, but forEach doesn't wait for any of them. It starts every callback, ignores the promises they return, and moves on. The toast shows while the uploads are still running.

Two fixes:
for...of with await uploads one file at a time, in order.
await Promise.all(files.map(upload)) uploads them in parallel and waits for all of them.

Pick in order when the server cares about order, parallel when it doesn't.

Source: MDN, Array.prototype.forEach() (it expects a synchronous function).

card.text:
AI isn't replacing junior developers.

It's replacing juniors who [[can't explain their own code]].

caption:
Using AI to write code is normal now. Teams expect it.

What gets noticed in a code review or an interview is whether you understand what got written. Why this hook, why this query, what happens when the API fails.

One habit fixes most of it: before you commit AI-written code, explain each line to yourself out loud.

If you can't, you're not done yet.

card.text:
Your users aren't on your laptop.

DevTools → Network → [[Slow 4G]]
Performance → CPU: [[4x slowdown]]

Now load your app. That's closer to a budget Android phone.

caption:
Your laptop has a fast CPU and fast Wi-Fi. A lot of your users have neither.

Throttling in DevTools isn't a perfect copy of a real phone, but it shows the problems quickly: a blank screen while JavaScript downloads, buttons that don't respond, a spinner that never ends.

Fix the biggest one you notice. Then test on a real low-end phone if you can borrow one.

Source: Chrome DevTools docs, Network and CPU throttling.

card.title:
buildIndex runs on every keystroke.
The result is thrown away. Why?
card.note: Pass the [[function]], not its result, and React calls it only once.

caption:
The AI wrote correct code that does a lot of work for nothing. Would you catch it in review?

Look at the card. buildIndex(products) is an ordinary function call. JavaScript runs it every time the component renders, before useState even sees it. React uses the value on the first render and ignores it after that. So the index gets rebuilt on every keystroke and thrown away.

Pass a function instead: useState(() => buildIndex(products)). React calls it only on the first render.

This only matters when the initial value is expensive to create: parsing, sorting, building a lookup. For useState(0) there's nothing to save.

Source: react.dev, useState (avoiding recreating the initial state).

card.title:
Switch from Asha's profile to Ravi's.
Why does the form still say Asha?

panels.label: Common answer

card.note: useState reads its argument [[once]]. A new key gives a fresh component.

caption:
This one catches people who know hooks well.

Look at the card. EditProfile copies user.name into state. When the parent passes a different user, the component stays in the same place in the tree, so React keeps its state. The initial value is only read on the first render. The input keeps showing Asha.

The cleanest fix is on the parent: key={user.id}. A different key tells React it's a different component, so it throws the old state away and starts fresh with Ravi.

You don't need a useEffect that syncs the prop into state. That version renders the wrong name first and then corrects it.

Source: react.dev, Preserving and Resetting State.

card.text:
Interviewers forget the 10 projects you listed.

They remember [[the one you could defend]].

caption:
A resume with ten tutorial projects reads like a list.

One project you built properly gives you everything an interview needs: decisions you made, trade-offs you chose, a bug you hunted down, a number that improved.

Go deep on one. Be ready to answer "why did you build it this way?" for every part of it.

card.text:
AI writes the first draft.

[[You own the last one.]]

caption:
When AI-written code breaks in production, nobody blames the AI. The name on the commit is yours.

So treat its output like a pull request from a fast, confident intern: useful, often right, and always worth reading before it ships.

Test the edge cases, read the diff, and make sure you could debug it at 2 AM without help.

card.title:
AI renders the comment as HTML.
Would you merge this?
card.note: React escapes text for you. That one prop [[turns it off]].

caption: The AI wanted line breaks and bold text in comments, so it rendered them as HTML. It works, and it's a security hole. Look at the card. When you write {comment.text}, React escapes it, so any HTML tags show up as plain text. dangerouslySetInnerHTML skips that. If someone posts a comment like , the browser runs that code for every person who views the page. That's XSS (cross-site scripting). If you really need formatted comments, convert them on purpose (a markdown library) and sanitize the HTML with a library like DOMPurify before rendering. The prop is named "dangerously" for a reason. Treat it as a review flag. Source: react.dev, Common components (dangerouslySetInnerHTML).

card.title:
Deep copy with JSON.
Why is the date now a string?

panels.label: Common answer

card.note: JSON keeps text and numbers. [[structuredClone]] keeps real types.

caption:
"How do you deep copy an object?" If your answer is JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()), expect a follow-up.

Look at the card. JSON.stringify turns a Date into a string, and JSON.parse doesn't turn it back. So copy.placedAt is a string and getTime() throws. The same trip silently drops undefined values and functions, and turns a Map or Set into an empty object.

structuredClone is built into modern browsers and Node 17+. It copies Dates, Maps, Sets and nested objects properly. It throws on functions instead of dropping them quietly.

JSON is still fine for plain data that came from an API.

Source: MDN, structuredClone().

card.text:
Stop asking "which framework should I learn?"

Start asking "[[which problem do I want to solve?]]"

caption:
The framework question has no right answer, so it keeps you stuck.

A problem has a clear next step. Want to build a tool for your college fest? You'll learn forms, auth and a database because you need them.

Frameworks change every few years. Knowing how to pick a tool for a problem doesn't go out of date.

card.text:
You have one year. Pick one:

A) Go deep in React and frontend
B) Become full-stack: React + Node + Postgres

[[Which one, and why?]]

caption:
Both paths get people hired. They lead to different kinds of roles.

Deep frontend leads to specialist roles: performance, design systems, complex UIs.
Full-stack opens more doors at startups, where one person often owns a feature end to end.

What would you pick, and what are you basing it on: job listings, your college, or what you enjoy building?

card.title:
Quantity 2, add 1.
Why does the cart say 21?
card.note: An input's value is [[always a string]], even with type="number".

caption:
The AI built a quantity picker with type="number" and assumed it gives you a number. It doesn't.

Look at the card. input.value is always a string. type="number" only changes the keyboard and the validation. So qty is "2", and "2" + 1 is string concatenation: "21".

Number inputs have valueAsNumber, which returns a real number. It returns NaN when the field is empty, so handle that case before you do math with it. Number(e.target.value) works too.

The same is true for every form field: values come in as strings. Convert at the edge, as soon as you read them.

Source: MDN, input type="number" (value and valueAsNumber).

card.title:
₹0.10 + ₹0.20.
Why isn't the total ₹0.30?

panels.label: What gets you selected

card.note: Keep money in [[whole paise]]. Convert to rupees only to display it.

caption:
Build a cart in a machine coding round, add prices as decimals, and a total like 0.30000000000000004 appears on screen.

Look at the card. JavaScript numbers are binary floating point. 0.1 and 0.2 can't be stored exactly in binary, so their sum is a tiny bit off. That's true in most languages, not just JavaScript.

The fix most payment systems use: store amounts as integers in the smallest unit. ₹499.50 becomes 49950 paise. Integer addition is exact.

Convert only when you show the amount. Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' }) formats it with the ₹ sign and Indian digit grouping.

Source: MDN, Number (number encoding).

card.text:
Learning 5 frameworks a little
< learning [[how the browser works]] properly.

caption:
Every frontend framework runs on the same browser: the DOM, events, the network, rendering, the JavaScript event loop.

Once you understand those, a new framework is just a new way of writing things you already know.

If you only know one framework's syntax, every new one feels like starting over.

card.text:
Submit your login form with JavaScript turned off.

Does the [[password]] show up in the URL?

caption:
A <form> with no method attribute sends its data with GET. GET puts every field in the URL, password included. URLs end up in browser history, server logs and analytics tools.

Usually JavaScript intercepts the submit, so you never notice. But if your script fails to load or throws before preventDefault runs, the browser does the default.

The fix is one attribute: method="post" on the form. Add it even when JavaScript handles the submit.

Source: MDN, The Form element (method attribute).

card.title:
AI wrote this fetch.
Why is the Network tab on fire?
card.note: No dependency array means [[after every render]]. Including the one it caused.

caption:
The AI wrote this, it works, and your backend team is about to message you.

Look at the card. With no dependency array, the effect runs after every render. It fetches the user and calls setUser with a new object. A new object means a re-render. The re-render runs the effect again. That's an endless loop of requests.

The fix is one argument: an empty array, so the effect runs once on mount. If the request depends on a value, like an id, put that value in the array.

React won't warn you about this one. The Network tab will.

Source: react.dev, useEffect (dependencies).

card.title:
Works while logged in.
Crashes the moment you log out. Why?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: Hooks must run in the [[same order]] on every render. No early return before them.

caption:
An early return before a hook is a classic machine coding mistake. It works until the condition flips.

Look at the card. While user exists, Cart calls useState. When the user logs out, the function returns before reaching useState. React tracks hooks by their call order, so it sees fewer hooks than last time and throws "Rendered fewer hooks than expected".

The rule: call every hook at the top level, before any return. Put conditions after the hooks, or move the logged-out branch into the parent.

The eslint-plugin-react-hooks rules-of-hooks check flags this as you type.

Source: react.dev, Rules of Hooks.

card.text:
AI made writing code faster.

It made [[debugging]] the skill that gets you hired.

caption:
If everyone can generate code in minutes, writing it stops being what sets you apart.

Finding out why it breaks in production still takes a person who can read logs, reproduce bugs and reason about state.

Practise it on purpose. Next time something breaks, don't paste the error into AI straight away. Spend 15 minutes on it yourself first.

card.text:
Prompting isn't the skill.

[[Context]] is.

caption:
The same AI tool gives a junior and a senior very different results. Usually it's not the wording of the prompt.

The senior gives it the right files, the constraints, the existing patterns, the edge cases to handle and how to check the result.

That context comes from understanding the codebase. Which is why learning the codebase still matters more than learning prompt tricks.

card.title:
The first tag in the list
is never found. Why?
card.note: indexOf returns [[0]] for the first item. 0 is falsy, and -1 is truthy.

caption:
An AI wrote this check, and it's wrong in both directions.

Look at the card. indexOf returns a position. If 'sale' is the first tag, it returns 0, and 0 is falsy, so no badge. If 'sale' isn't there at all, it returns -1, and -1 is truthy, so the badge shows.

includes returns true or false, which is what an if statement needs.

If you really need indexOf, compare explicitly: indexOf('sale') !== -1.

Bugs like this pass a quick test because the first test case usually puts the value somewhere in the middle.

Source: MDN, Array.prototype.indexOf() and includes().

card.title:
['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt)
Why [1, NaN, NaN]?
card.note: map passes [[(value, index)]]. parseInt reads the index as a radix.

caption:
Interviewers love this one because it looks like it can't possibly fail.

Look at the card. map calls your function with three arguments: the value, the index and the array. parseInt takes two: the string and a radix (the number base).

So the calls are parseInt('1', 0), parseInt('2', 1) and parseInt('3', 2). A radix of 0 means "work it out", so '1' gives 1. Base 1 doesn't exist, so NaN. In base 2 only 0 and 1 are digits, so '3' gives NaN.

Fix: map(Number), or wrap it so you control the arguments, with a radix of 10.

Source: MDN, parseInt() and Array.prototype.map().

card.text:
Your degree gets you the interview.

[[What you built]] gets you the offer.

caption:
College name and CGPA help you clear the resume filter. That's their job.

Once you're in the room, the questions are about what you've done. Something you built, a problem you solved, a decision you can defend.

If your projects section is empty, that's the place to spend this semester.

card.text:
One year into your first job. Pick one:

A) Switch now for a 40% hike
B) Stay one more year under a senior who teaches you a lot

[[What would you do?]]

caption:
Both are reasonable. The hike is real money. The senior is rare, and a good one can change how you work for years.

Some things worth weighing: will the new role teach you as much? Does your current team still have things to teach you? Do you need the money now?

If you've faced this choice, which way did you go, and would you do it again?

card.title:
z-index: 9999.
Still behind the header. Why?

panels.label: AI-generated

card.note: transform starts a new [[stacking context]]. 9999 only counts inside it.

caption:
The AI kept raising the z-index. The dropdown stayed behind the sticky header.

Look at the card. transform on .card creates a new stacking context. Inside it, the menu's z-index of 9999 is compared only with other things inside .card. The card as a whole sits below the header, which has z-index 10 at the page level, so the menu goes under it.

opacity below 1, filter and will-change can do the same thing.

The robust fix: render the menu outside the card. createPortal mounts it under document.body, so its z-index competes at the page level. Or remove the transform if you don't need it.

Source: MDN, Stacking context.

card.title:
Tab through the page.
Why can't you reach Add to cart?
card.note: A div with onClick looks like a button. Only a [[button]] behaves like one.

caption:
Senior frontend rounds now include accessibility questions, and this is the first one.

Look at the card. The div looks right and works with a mouse. But a div can't take keyboard focus, so Tab skips it. Enter and Space don't trigger it. A screen reader announces it as plain text, not as a button.

A real button gives you all of that for free: focus, keyboard activation and the right role.

Patching the div needs tabIndex, role="button" and a keydown handler for Enter and Space. That's three things to get right instead of one tag.

Quick test for your own project: unplug the mouse and try to buy something.

Source: MDN, ARIA button role (prefer the button element).

card.text:
Before you "learn AI",
learn to [[read an error message]] all the way to the end.

caption:
Most error messages tell you what went wrong and where. The file, the line, often the fix.

A lot of beginners read the first line, panic and paste it somewhere.

Read the whole stack trace once. Find the first line that points at your own code. That habit alone will make you faster than half your batch.

card.text:
Run a bundle analyzer on your app once.

Most apps find [[one library]] taking a big slice of the bundle for one small feature.

caption:
A bundle analyzer draws your JavaScript bundle as a map of boxes, sized by how much each library adds.

Common finds: a whole date library to format one date, a full icon pack for five icons, a charting library loaded on pages without charts.

Try rollup-plugin-visualizer for Vite or @next/bundle-analyzer for Next.js. Then replace, trim or lazy-load the biggest box you don't really need.

Fewer kilobytes means a faster first load, especially on mobile data.

Source: the rollup-plugin-visualizer and @next/bundle-analyzer READMEs.

card.title:
The API sent a 500 with a JSON error.
Why didn't catch run?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: fetch only rejects when the [[network]] fails. A 404 or 500 still resolves.

caption:
The AI wrapped fetch in try/catch and called it error handling. Would you merge it?

Look at the card. fetch rejects only when the request can't complete at all: no network, DNS failure, CORS block. A 404 or 500 is a complete response, so fetch resolves normally with res.ok set to false.

Here the server sends a 500 with a JSON body like { message: "..." }. res.json() parses it fine, and render() tries to draw an error object as if it were real data. catch never runs.

Check res.ok (true for status 200-299) and throw yourself when it's false. Libraries like axios reject on non-2xx statuses by default, which is why people coming from axios miss this.

Source: MDN, Using the Fetch API (checking that the fetch was successful).

card.title:
Why does this print 3 3 3
instead of 0 1 2?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: [[let]] gives every loop iteration its own i. var shares one.

caption:
Still one of the most asked JavaScript output questions in frontend interviews.

Look at the card. With var there is one i for the whole loop. The timeouts run after the loop has finished, and by then i is 3. All three callbacks read the same variable, so they all print 3.

With let, each iteration gets a new binding of i. Each callback closes over its own copy: 0, 1 and 2.

Interviewers usually follow up with "how would you fix it without let?" Before ES6 the answer was an IIFE (a function you call immediately) that passes i in as a parameter.

Source: MDN, let (scoping rules) and Closures.

card.text:
Every senior developer you admire
has [[broken production]] at least once.

caption:
Seniors aren't people who never make mistakes. They've made more of them, and learned how to recover calmly.

They roll back, communicate, find the cause and write it down so it doesn't happen again.

If you broke something at your first job, you're not bad at this. You've just started collecting the stories seniors tell.

card.text:
Practise [[reviewing code]] as seriously as you practise writing it.

That's most of the job now.

caption:
More code is generated every month. Someone still has to decide what gets merged.

Reviewing is a skill: spotting the missing edge case, the unnecessary re-render, the security hole that "works fine".

Easy way to practise: open a merged pull request in a popular open source repo, read the diff, write down what you'd ask, then read the real review comments.

card.title:
Add a seat to row 1.
Why did every row get it?
card.note: fill puts the [[same array]] in every slot. Array.from builds a new one each time.

caption:
An AI built a seat map for a booking page. Book one seat and every row shows it.

Look at the card. fill([]) creates one empty array and puts that same array in all three slots. rows[0], rows[1] and rows[2] all point to it, so a push through any of them shows up in all of them.

Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => []) calls the function once per slot, so each row gets its own array.

The same trap applies to fill({}) with objects. fill(0) or fill('') is fine, because numbers and strings aren't shared references.

Source: MDN, Array.prototype.fill() (filling with an object).

card.title:
Three API calls take 3 seconds.
They could take 1. How?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: Independent requests shouldn't [[wait in line]].

caption:
If a dashboard takes 3 seconds to load in your machine coding round, check for this first.

Look at the card. Each await waits for the previous request to finish before the next one starts. If each call takes about a second, the page waits about three. That's a request waterfall.

None of the three needs data from the others, so start them together. Promise.all waits for all of them, and the total is roughly the slowest one.

If one request is allowed to fail without breaking the page, use Promise.allSettled instead.

Only keep them in sequence when one really needs the result of another.

Source: MDN, Promise.all().

card.text:
A ₹2 LPA hike to learn something new
beats a ₹4 LPA hike to [[do the same work for 3 more years]].

caption:
Early in your career, what you learn compounds faster than salary does.

A role that stretches you raises what you're worth on every job change after it. A role that only pays more can leave you with three years of the same experience, repeated.

Not always true. If your family needs the money now, that matters more than any rule. But ask the question before you sign.

card.text:
Placements start in 4 months.
This weekend, pick one:

A) Solve 20 DSA problems
B) Finish the project you started

[[Which one, and why?]]

caption:
Students ask this every placement season, and the honest answer depends on the companies you're targeting.

Some rounds are mostly DSA. Others care more about projects and how you explain them.

If you've been through placements recently: what actually helped more in your interviews?

card.title:
The Pay button is hidden on phones.
Only on phones. Why?
card.note: On phones, 100vh is the height [[with the toolbars hidden]]. dvh tracks the real height.

caption:
The AI built a full-height checkout. On a laptop it's perfect. On a phone the Pay button sits under the browser's address bar.

Look at the card. On mobile browsers, 100vh is the viewport height when the browser toolbars are hidden. While they're showing, the page is taller than the visible area, and anything pinned to the bottom ends up under the toolbar.

dvh (dynamic viewport height) follows the visible area as the toolbars appear and disappear. svh is the smallest size, if you'd rather it never change.

All major browsers support these units. Test on a real phone, not just in DevTools device mode.

Source: MDN, CSS length units (viewport units: lvh, svh, dvh).

card.title:
The page jumps while it loads.
Which line causes it?

panels.label: What gets you selected

card.note: [[width and height]] let the browser save space before the image arrives.

caption:
You tap a button, the banner finishes loading, everything shifts down, and you tap the wrong thing. That's layout shift, and Google measures it as CLS.

Look at the card. Without width and height, the browser doesn't know how tall the image will be. It gives it zero height, then pushes the content down when the image arrives.

With width and height, the browser works out the aspect ratio before downloading anything and reserves the right space. CSS can still make it responsive with width: 100% and height: auto.

Check yours: DevTools, Performance panel, record a reload and look for layout shifts.

Source: web.dev, Optimize Cumulative Layout Shift.

card.text:
The fastest way to grow at your first job:

[[sit near the person who fixes production]].

caption:
Watch how they debug. Which dashboards they open, which logs they read, what they check first.

Offer to help with the boring parts of an incident. Read the write-up afterwards.

You'll learn more about how real systems fail in one week of that than in a month of tutorials.

card.text:
Paste your project's link into a WhatsApp chat.

No title, no image, just a bare URL?

You're missing [[Open Graph tags]].

caption:
When someone shares a link, WhatsApp, LinkedIn and most chat apps read Open Graph meta tags to build the preview card: og:title, og:description and og:image.

Without them, your portfolio or project shows up as a plain link that nobody taps.

Add the three tags to your page's <head>, with an image around 1200x630. If your app renders on the client only, make sure those tags are in the HTML the server sends, because link preview bots usually don't run JavaScript.

Recruiters open links from chats too.

Source: ogp.me (The Open Graph protocol).

card.title:
AI lazy-loaded every image.
Why did the page get slower?
card.note: Lazy-load what's [[below the fold]]. The hero image is your LCP.

caption:
An AI was asked to "optimize images" and put loading="lazy" on all of them, including the big banner at the top.

Look at the card. Lazy loading tells the browser to wait until it knows the image is near the viewport. For the hero image, which is usually the Largest Contentful Paint (when the biggest thing on screen appears), that delay is exactly what you don't want. LCP gets worse.

Load the hero eagerly, which is the default, and add fetchpriority="high" so the browser fetches it before less important resources. In React the prop is fetchPriority.

Keep loading="lazy" for images further down the page.

Source: web.dev, Browser-level image lazy loading (avoid lazy-loading images in the first visible viewport).
